name: Samoa
summary: Western Samoa was German (1900–14), then ruled by New Zealand; in 1962 it became the first Pacific island nation to win independence.

location.value: South Pacific; land area 2,842 km² in the text, 2,831 km² in the infobox and 2,934 km² in a farming passage, so the figures conflict.

terrain.value: Volcanic islands with rugged mountainous interiors, rainforest and coastal plains; Savai’i rises to about 1,860 m at Mount Silisili.

climate.value: Hot and humid tropical climate, with a wet season from about November to April when cyclones can strike.

resources.value: Fertile volcanic soil for coconuts, taro and bananas, fish, tropical timber, and beaches and scenery that draw tourists.

disasters.value: Cyclones Ofa (1990), Val (1991) and Evan (2012) caused heavy damage, and the 2009 tsunami killed over 140 people in Samoa.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural villages; Apia on Upolu is the capital and only town, home to roughly 35,000–40,000 people.

disease.value: 1918 flu killed about a fifth of the people.

migration.value: Many live in New Zealand, Australia and the US.

economicBase.value: Agriculture employs two-thirds of the workforce and provides 90% of exports; tourism was about 20% of GDP in 2024 (24.5% in 2019). Remittances are not covered in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea and air links mainly with New Zealand, Australia and American Samoa; Faleolo International Airport serves Upolu.

moneyAndTax.value: The tālā (Samoan dollar), introduced in 1967; the government also collects a value-added goods and services tax.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary parliamentary republic with a 51-seat Fono; 49 seats go to matai (chiefly title-holders) and only matai can stand for them. Universal suffrage was adopted in 1990.

keyRulers.value: Samoa’s heads of state and prime ministers since independence in 1962 are not named here.

succession.value: Elections to the Fono choose the government; the Fono elects the head of state (O le Ao o le Malo) for five-year terms.

institutions.value: The Fono (Legislative Assembly), village councils of matai that govern local life, and the Land and Titles Court.

stability.value: Generally stable and democratic; the 1920s–30s Mau movement campaigned peacefully for independence, and a 2021 constitutional crisis was settled by the courts.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: No army: Samoa has a police force and a patrol boat, and the 1962 Treaty of Friendship lets it ask New Zealand for help.

majorWars.value: No wars since independence; before it, Samoan civil wars among rival chiefs (1880s–1899) drew in Germany, Britain and the US.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Samoa; Britannica: history of Samoa (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica describes factional wars among matai without dates, and dates the German and US annexations to 1899)

territoryChange.value: Islands divided between Germany and the US (1899).

alliancesRivals.value: Close ties with New Zealand through the 1962 Treaty of Friendship; joined the Commonwealth (1970), the UN (1976) and the Pacific Islands Forum.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The National University of Samoa (founded 1984) and a University of the South Pacific campus at Alafua; literacy is high.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Ferries between Upolu and Savai’i across the Apolima Strait, buses, and flights from Faleolo; in 2009 Samoa switched to driving on the left.

religion.value: 2021: Christian 97.9% (Protestant 54.9%, Catholic 18.8%, Mormon 16.9%); Parliament made Christianity the state religion in 2017.

languageWriting.value: Samoan, a Polynesian language spoken by nearly everyone and written in the Latin alphabet since missionaries arrived in the 1830s, and English.

artsArchitecture.value: Tatau (traditional tattooing), siapo bark cloth, fine mats (’ie tōga), open-sided fale houses and siva dance.

socialStructure.value: Fa’amatai: extended families (aiga) led by chosen matai chiefs, who hold family land and speak for the family in village councils.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Samoan identity built on fa’a Samoa (the Samoan way), the matai system, church and language.

dailyLife.value: Village life centres on family, church and the umu (earth oven); taro, breadfruit, fish and palusami (taro leaves in coconut cream) are staples.

neighbours.value: American Samoa (a US territory) to the east, Tonga to the south, Fiji to the south-west and Tokelau to the north.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity, brought by London Missionary Society missionaries from 1830, combined with fa’a Samoa and respect for the matai.

colonisation.value: The German Empire governed western Samoa from 1900 to 1914; New Zealand then controlled it until 1962 as a Class C Mandate.

riseSignals.value: The Lapita people settled the Samoan Islands around 3,500 years ago; the earliest human remains are dated 2,900 to 3,500 years ago. Britannica dates Lapita pottery at Mulifanua to about 1000 BCE, which is nearer 3,000 years ago.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Samoa (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: history of Samoa (checked 15 Nov 2026) (it does not mention 3,500 years)

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; growth in tourism and remittances since the 1990s has raised living standards.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Independence as Western Samoa, effective 1 January 1962.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Samoa (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: history of Samoa (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica gives 1962 for independence; the day is not on the page)

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
